messages.subject: Truncation of data with few observations?
messages.subject_clean: Truncation of data with few observations?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance samplers
I have been analysing data from a survey on long-tailed macaques and Javan lutung for some time...
I have now gone through all key functions with all series expansions.
I have tried grouping, yet grouping yields the same results as ungrouped data for both species.
Data has been added as clusters (sub-groups) for both animals.
To avoid double counting, we have only included our outbound trip for both species.

Buckland et al, 2001 recommend a 5% truncation, and around or above 80 observations.
For Javan lutung we only have 40 observations, and with a 5% truncation that reduces to 38.
For long-tailed macaques we have sufficient observations.
For both species estimated density and abundance increases a lot with truncation (eg. lutung: no truncation: 9ind/km2, 150m truncation: 11ind/km2, 5% truncation: 14ind/km2)
We conducted the survey in a very diverse area with many different habitats, this means that in savanna areas we can see as far as 500m but in others we may only be able to see 10m away.

Half normal key seems to fit the best for both species under all conditions, but the 5% truncation yields the best GOF results (not in comparison of course, but highest non-significant p. values), however the 150m truncation (removing 1 observation for both species at 250m) also seems to yeild good results with the half normal key. For the 5% truncation teh half normal key uses 2 cosine adjustments, for the 150m truncation there are no adjustments.
The reason to choose 150m as truncation is that is seems to be our limit of observations except for one observation (250m), and it only removes one oservation from both datasets.
Our w seems to be approx 65 for both species, yet with 65m as truncation distance the density increases even more (Javan lutung 16ind/km2).

There are no current density estimates on long-tailed macaques, and only one on Javan lutung (9ind/km2), so not a lot to compare to....

I am unsure of which truncation to use for my data, if any at all?
I hope you can help.
Please aks if you have any questions.
Thank you for reading this :)
Malene

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Truncation of data with few observations?
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Truncation of data with few observations?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Malene, list

With the information you provide is not possible to provide feedback. The right distance to truncate especially in small data sets might be quite hard to choose - ideally you want the results to be insensitive to the choice. The fact that density estimates change considerably depending on the truncation used implies there's something that we need to understand better before knowing what might be the best approach. Can you please send histograms of the data for visual inspection. Feel free to send those separately just to me and not the list. If we conclude something you can then post some conclusions to the list.

The aspect that worries me the most in your description is the extreme habitat heterogeneity in terms of detection, which could lead to problems. I suspect that if "in savanna areas we can see as far as 500m but in others we may only be able to see 10m away ", that might correspond to a level of heterogeneity that will cause pooling robustness to collapse.

Cheers,

Tiago

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Re: Error in predict.ds
messages.body_plain:
Isabel

Without your dataset, I tried to reconstruct your problem using the "golftee" data included in the mrds package.  As you are using single observer data (method="ds"), I use the example code provided with the function ddf.ds(), adding a couple of lines to make sex and size factor covariates (as you have covariates in your detection function):

data(book.tee.data)
region <- book.tee.data$book.tee.region
egdata <- book.tee.data$book.tee.dataframe
samples <- book.tee.data$book.tee.samples
obs <- book.tee.data$book.tee.obs
egdata$size <- as.factor(egdata$size)
egdata$sex <- as.factor(egdata$sex)
result <- ddf(dsmodel = ~mcds(key = "hn", formula = ~sex+size),
              data = egdata[egdata$observer==1, ], method = "ds",
              meta.data = list(width = 4))
summary(result,se=TRUE)
plot(result,main="cds - observer 1")
my.pred <- predict(result, newdata=egdata[egdata$observer==1,], esw=TRUE)
> head(my.pred$fitted)
[1] 2.475936 2.475936 1.534598 2.475936 2.475936 3.876284

As you see, I cannot reproduce the problem you report.

Are you treating the covariates in your model as factors or continuous variables; perhaps check there.
